Ferdinand Magellan. A Portuguese explorer who led the first expedition to circumnavigate the globe, though he died before its completion. Born around 1480, Magellan sailed for the Spanish crown seeking a westward route to the Spice Islands, a voyage that proved the true scope of Earth's oceans and established Spain's colonial claim to the Philippines.

Born in Portugal, Magellan served the Portuguese crown in India and Malaysia, but quarreled with the Portuguese king and offered his services to Spain. He persuaded King Charles the Fifth to fund a westward expedition to the Spice Islands. Departing Spain in September 1519 with five ships and roughly two hundred seventy men, he discovered the Strait of Magellan at the southern tip of South America, a crucial waterway allowing passage to the Pacific Ocean.

He named the Pacific Ocean Mar Pacifico, the Peaceful Sea, for its apparent calm after months at sea. He crossed the vast ocean largely without resupply, enduring starvation and scurvy. Magellan reached the Philippines in March 1521 and was killed on April 27, 1521, during a skirmish on the island of Mactan against indigenous chief Lapu-Lapu in a battle over Spanish authority.

Though Magellan died, his expedition continued under the command of Juan Sebastián Elcano, who returned one ship to Spain in 1522 with eighteen survivors. They were the first to complete a circumnavigation. The expedition's achievement proved Earth was far larger than previously believed, established the vastness of the Pacific, and demonstrated the feasibility of global sea routes, reshaping navigation and geography forever.
